# Native references and copy-out destinations (SIM-008)

The task module runs every positive fixture through the public CLI in both HDL
optimizer modes on legacy, compact/portable and compact/GMP values. Expected outputs are derived by hand from the
cited clauses, not captured from llg.

| Fixture | Clause and independent oracle |
| --- | --- |
| `element_copy_out` | §§7.8, 7.10, 13.5.1-13.5.2. (1) `outq(q[1])` stores 7 after the call: `1 7`. (2) The inout `q[0]` copies in 1 and back 11. (3) Output into a string-keyed associative element stores 7 into the existing `y` and creates `z`: `7 7 2`. (4) An inout of an existing integral-keyed element: 1 + 10 = 11. (5) A real queue element receives 2.5. (6) `d[k]` with `k = 1` writes the second element: `0 7`. (7) The timed task's copy-out target `q[k]` is evaluated when the value is copied out (decision S13-D1): `k` became 1 and `push_front(9)` made the queue 9 11 7, so the copy-out after `#1` stores 3 at index 1: `9 3 7` (changed: the index was frozen at the call, giving `3 11 7`). |
| `container_refs` | §§7.10, 9.2.2.2, 13.5.2. (1) The forked task pushes 9 through its `ref` before the parent's `#0` display: size 2, `q[1]` = 9, and `always_comb` already sees 2. (2) After its `#1` the task writes the current size into `q[0]`: 2. (3) A string queue gains `z` in front: `2 z`. (4) Two refs to the same queue: the push through `a` is visible through `b`: 3. (5) An associative ref creates key `k`: 3. Some simulators do not re-evaluate `always_comb` when a queue changes size (`seen` stays 0); llg follows 9.2.2.2.1 L11184-11185 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "The implicit sensitivity list of an always_comb includes the expansions of the longest static prefix of each variable or select expression that is read within the block", and `q` is read there. |
| `element_refs` | §§13.5.2, 7.10.3. (1) `d[1]` held by a timed task sees the parent's write of 5 at time 1 and its own write of 6 reaches `d` and `always_comb` (6 6); `new[5](d)` at time 3 outdates it, so the write of 9 stays private while `d[1]` keeps the copied 6 and the size is 5. (2) `aa[3]` sees 7 then writes 8 into `aa`; after `aa.delete(3)` the write of 11 does not recreate the entry. (3) A ref to a missing string key creates it on write: `1 4`. (4) Two refs to `d[0]` share the outdated element after `d.delete()`: 3, size 0. (5) `q.delete(0)` leaves the ref to the old `q[2]` live, so 99 lands in the new `q[1]`. (6) A ref to an element beyond the bounds reads the default and ignores writes: `0 0`. Some simulators do not re-evaluate `always_comb` after a write to a dynamic-array element (`seen` stays 2; 9.2.2.2.1 L11184-11185 includes the longest static prefix `d` of `d[1]`), and stop the run at a `ref` actual that selects an element of an empty array; llg applies 7.4.6 L8235-8237: "The result of reading from an array with an invalid index shall return the default uninitialized value for the array element type. Writing to an array with an invalid index shall perform no operation." Element bindings across `delete`, `push_front`, `insert`, whole assignments and `new[]` agree. |
| `string_element_refs` | §§7.8, 7.10.3, 13.5.1, 13.5.2. String elements of fixed (also descending and 2-D), queue, dynamic and associative arrays as `ref`, `const ref`, `inout` and `output` actuals. 7.10.3 L9154-9156: "a reference to any existing element that is not deleted by the method shall not become outdated", so the reference follows `push_front`, `insert`, `reverse` and `sort` (B1-B5) until `pop_front`/`delete` remove its element (B7-B9: writes stay private); L9158-9159 outdates a whole queue assignment (C), 13.5.2 L19161-19167 a resized dynamic array (G) and a deleted entry (E3-E4: a new entry of that key stays apart), and a fixed array's element is the same variable across a whole assignment (D). A new associative assignment outdates too (F). Index and key are taken at the call (`late(fs[l])`). A binding creates a missing entry, also for `const ref` (decision S13-D2). Stores of every string form reach the element at once (`stores`); class-property, automatic and forwarded elements bind the same way; a `disable` releases the reference. The output agrees with industry-standard behaviour. |
| `string_element_refs_invalid` | §7.4.6 L8235-8237: an invalid selector reads the default and a write does nothing, as `element_refs` (6) does for packed elements. Some simulators stop the run at such a `ref` actual. |
| `record_refs` | §13.5.2. `bump(l, l)` increments `a` to 2, appends `!` and pushes 2 through `r`, and `other` sees all three: `2 x! 1`. The timed `hold` writes 40 and `late` into the caller's record after `#1`; `peek` reads through a `const ref`: 40 + 1 queue element = 41. |
| `module_record_refs` | §§13.5.2, 13.5.1, 6.21, 7.2, 10.5. The static initializer `made = grab(seed)` copies {3, `seed`}, adds 1 and renames `seed` through the ref: `init 4 seed taken`. `forward(g)`: `pair(r, r)` increments `a` to 2 and appends `+` through the other ref (`pair 2 g+`); `take(r, tmp, r)` copies in {2, `g+`}, outputs `a` = 20 into `tmp` and copies the inout back as 2 + 2 = 4 (`tmp 20 g+ 0`); `take(tmp, r, tmp)` with `tmp.s` = `tmp` outputs 20 * 10 = 200 and `tmp` into `g`; `r.h = new(200)`, `r.r` = 1.75; the package task appends `!` and pushes the old size 0: `g 200 tmp! 1.75 200 0 201 tmp!/200` (`weight` = 200 + 1, `label` through a string-returning `const ref` function). The static block record `sb` = {5, `sb`} and `g2` = {7, `g2`}: `pair(sb, g2)` gives `pair 7 sb` and leaves 6 and `g2+`; `swap` exchanges them: `swap g2+ 7 sb 6 0`; after `sb = g2` the two compare equal: `same 1`. The automatic block record restarts empty each iteration: i = 0 gives `pair 1 a+`, `ab 1 a+ 1`; i = 1 gives `pair 2 a+`, `ab 2 a+ 1`. Member actuals `o.in` and `o.arr[1]`: `pair 0 i`, then `stamp(o.arr[0], "z")`: `o 4 i e+ z 1`. One step later `always_comb` gives `weight(g)` = 201 and the continuous assignment `weight(g2)` = 6 + 0. |
| `timed_record_refs` | §§9.2.2.2, 9.4.2, 9.4.3, 9.6.2, 13.5.2. `worker(g)` writes `a` = 1 at 0; at 1 the parent sees `D 1 10` (`always_comb seen` = 10 * a) and writes 5 and `p`; at 2 the task sees them: `A 5 p 50`, then writes 7 and pushes 3; at 3 the parent sees `E 7 70 1` and writes `q`, which wakes `@(r.s)`: `B q 3`; at 4 the parent writes 9, which ends `wait (r.a == 9)`: `C 9`; after `#0`, `F q q 90` (`always @(g.s)` copied `q`). `mirror(g2, g2)` writes 100 through `x`, the parent adds 1 at 5, and `z` reads `G 101` at 6. `disable slowset` at 7 keeps the write of 1 made before its delay: `H 1`. `countdown(g3, 3)` (join_none) pushes 3, 2, 1 in front at 6, 7 and 8: `I 3 1 3` at 11. The automatic block record `ab` = 1 gains 10 through `later` at 12: `J 11` at 13. Each `unit` instance binds its own record: P = 1 starts at 12 and adds 1 at 13 and 14 (`tb.u1 2 u1 2` at 15, `always_comb mseen` = 2); P = 3 starts at 16 (`tb.u2 6 u3 6` at 19). Some simulators do not re-evaluate `always_comb` after a write to a record member (`seen` stays 10, `mseen` 0); llg follows 9.2.2.2.1 L11184-11185 (`SystemVerilog-1800-2009.txt`): "The implicit sensitivity list of an always_comb includes the expansions of the longest static prefix of each variable or select expression that is read within the block". |
| `record_element_refs` | §§7.10.3, 13.5.2. Record elements of fixed (also 2-D), queue, dynamic and associative arrays, nested records and members bind `ref` and `const ref` formals of tasks, functions in expressions and class methods, virtual ones included. Formal and element name one record: writes through either side are seen at once (C2-C5); the reference follows `push_front` and `reverse` and is outdated by `delete` (C7-C8), `pop_front` (P) and `new[]` (F); a fixed array's element stays bound across a whole assignment (E); a deleted associative entry stays apart (G). The output agrees with industry-standard behaviour. |
| `record_member_refs` | §13.5.2 L19143-19147 lists a member of an unpacked structure and an element of an unpacked array. A string, integer, handle and member-array element of a record element bind `ref` formals: (A) formal, member and record see each other's writes; (B) the member follows its element across `push_front`, a whole-element assignment reaches it, and after `delete` the formals keep the last values and stay private; (`index_at_call`) `k` changes after the bind, so `f[k]` stays `f[0]`, also for `f[1].a[k]`, `aa[3]` is created at the bind (S13-D2), and subroutine records and forwarded formals take run-time selections; (waits) writes to the element's member wake the formal's waits: the string at 5 and the integer at 7, not at the 2 written at 6; an invalid selection (`f[7]`, `a[9]`) reads the default and ignores writes (7.4.6 L8235-8237). Expected output derived by hand from these clauses; some simulators reject these actuals as unimplemented. |
| `record_ref_write_paths` | §§13.5.2, 9.4.3, decision S13-D4: each write path through a `ref` record formal bound to an array element, with its own array so nothing else can wake its waiter: intra-assignment delay and repeat event control, `for` init and step, task output and inout copy-out, function output in a condition, `x.n--` in a `while` condition (woken inside the loop, not after it), postfix and compound expressions, concatenation and streaming targets, string output, `$sformat`, `$swrite`, `putc`, `s[i]`, `itoa`, whole-record copies and record function results, real, handle, bit, part, nested and member-array stores, `foreach`, `$cast`, `$sscanf`, mailbox `get` of a member and a record, a nested `ref`, functions, a method and a record output. Reads through the formal publish nothing, so the `always_comb` reader runs once at 0. Expected output derived by hand from these clauses; some simulators reject the actual as unimplemented or wake only at a later string store. |
| `neg_record_ref_container_member` | Legal by §13.5.2; a record element with a queue member lacks the companion container its formal needs and is rejected explicitly. |
| `record_leaf_refs` | §13.5.2: `mr.t[i]`, `mr.a[i]` and handle or packed elements of module, static and block records as `ref` and `const ref` actuals. The index is taken once at the call; writes and waits follow the selected leaf. Agrees with industry-standard behaviour. |
| `record_leaf_ref_members` | §13.5.2, §7.4.6: members of run-time-indexed record elements (`mr.e[i].s`) and an index selecting no element, which reads the default and writes nowhere. Expected output derived from the clauses. |
| `record_method_refs` | §13.5.2: a module, static or block record, or a member of one, as the actual of a `ref` formal of a class method: direct, static, forwarded and virtual calls with overrides and `super`; writes reach the record at once and reads see other processes' stores across suspension. Agrees with industry-standard behaviour. |
| `record_method_ref_waits` | §13.5.2, §9.4.2: methods of a virtual family waiting on members of a module record `ref` actual, each override with its own wait. Agrees with industry-standard behaviour. |
| `record_ref_element_select` (FIN-001 G3) | §13.5.2 L19138-19141 ("both the caller and the subroutine share the same representation"), L19143-19147 ("an element of an unpacked array"); §7.4.6 for an index selecting no element. A run-time-selected record element of a module, static or block record binds a native record `ref` formal: the index is taken at the call (`timed` keeps element 1 after `i` moves, and an index with side effects runs once), stores reach the element at once and wake `@` readers, a task's `@(r.n)` wakes only for its element, also through recursion, forwarding, virtual and static methods and with two such actuals. An index selecting no element reads the default and drops writes. The queue-free subset agrees with industry-standard behaviour, except that some simulators do not wake `@(r.n)` here; forms with a queue member are not implemented elsewhere and are derived by hand from the clauses. |
| `record_ref_element_select_fatal` | A task waiting on the formal has no body without a binding, so an index selecting no element stops the run with a location, where §7.4.6 would give it a default record. |
| `neg_record_ref_element_select_limit`, `neg_record_ref_element_select_product`, `neg_record_ref_element_select_value` | Legal by §13.5.2, rejected explicitly: a call lowers once per element, so a site is bounded at 256 branches (`NATIVE_RECORD_SELECT_LIMIT`), and only statement calls can branch. |
| `neg_record_ref_interface_method` | Legal by §13.5.2; a module record bound to a virtual-interface method's `ref` formal rejects with an explicit diagnostic: the interface slot selects the implementation and no record binding can extend it. |
| `neg_record_ref_const_write` | Nearest illegal form (§13.5.2): a write through a `const ref` record formal is a frontend error. |
| `scan_elements` | §21.3.4.3. The first scan converts four items into `q[1]`, `d[0]`, `aa[3]` and `sa["k"]` (`41` hex = 65): `4 5 6 7 65`. The second converts only `aa[7]` = 9; `aa[8]` is never written, so it does not exist and `aa` holds keys 3 and 7: `1 9 0 2`. |
| `plusarg_elements` | §21.6, run with `+N=4 +H=1f`. `N` and `H` match into `q[0]` = 4 and `aa["h"]` = 'h1f = 31; `M` does not match, so `aa["m"]` is not created; `d[0]` = 4; three matches. |
| `mixed_ref_formals` | §13.5.2. `add(4, q)` and `add2(q, 5)` push through a queue `ref` declared after and before an input: 4 5; `set(3, l, "k")` writes a record through a `ref` between inputs: 3 + 1 = 4. `rec(2, r)` forwards its own `ref` queue to the recursive call after each `#1`; the innermost call prints first and each level keeps its own local queue: `0 0`, `1 1`, `2 2`, then `r` holds 3 elements at time 3. |
| `neg_expression_element_output` | A container element as an output actual of a call inside an expression is rejected at code generation (statement calls support it). |
